data.title: Canada Pins Hope for Economic Turbocharge on High-Profile Investor Summit — Analysis
data.description:
By Paul Vieira

OTTAWA--Deep-pocketed global investors descend on Toronto early next week at the invitation of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who is banking on their cash to help shift his restructuring of the country's economy into a higher gear.

Starting Monday, Carney hosts an investment summit that officials have likened to a matchmaking exercise, pairing companies pitching projects with some of the world's top asset managers responsible for assets totaling over $100 trillion. Wall Street heavyweights alongside sovereign-wealth and pension funds will size up over two days pitches for over 160 projects from Canadian executives in fields covering conventional and clean energy, mining, defense manufacturing, and power generation, according to a prospectus prepared for invitees and reviewed by The Wall Street Journal.

The gathering marks a high-profile push by Carney to rewire an economy that was struggling prior to the start of President Trump's second term, and which has been trying to navigate under the weight of hefty U.S. tariffs on key sectors and elevated uncertainty over preferential access to the world's biggest economy. Carney seeks to attract 1 trillion Canadian dollars (US$723 billion) over the next five years to build up economic resilience, and reshape a country that became too reliant and complacent on U.S. trade to drive growth.

Investors attending "are coming because of Canada. If they wanted to go to the United States, they go to the United States," Carney said. "What they are going to see when they come here is a country that is uniting, that is positive...and a country that respects rule of law and that is reliable--and that combination is pretty rare in the world."

Among the Canadian firms keen on cash at the summit is Deep Sky, a Montreal-based company that develops carbon-removal projects. The company is looking for $328 million from strategic investors to build its biggest carbon-capture and sequestration facility to date in oil-rich Alberta. Through its other facility, also in Alberta, Deep Sky has been able to sell carbon credits to Microsoft and other leading financing institutions, said Quentin Servais-Laval, the company's vice-president of finance.

The summit "will help put infrastructure projects that are shovel-ready in front of investors that have the funds to deploy and are really interested in the opportunity in Canada," Servais-Laval said, adding the company has meetings lined up in Toronto regarding its proposed plant. "So for me, it's an accelerator."

The summit comes at a crucial period for the Canadian economy, which recently showed signs of a breakthrough after 12 months of stagnant activity stemming from trade uncertainty. Economic ties between Canada and the U.S. have deteriorated in the past three weeks after talks toward a tariff deal collapsed, prompting both countries to impose new tariffs and restrictions on cross-border trade. On an individual-country basis, Canada is America's second-largest trading partner, with two-way annual trade of roughly $1 trillion.

A report published by Royal Bank of Canada said, based on analysis of United Nations data, Canada has attracted nearly 4% of global-inward foreign-direct investment, an admirable share for an economy that accounts for 2% of global output. "But relative to its potential--abundant resources, a highly educated workforce, and clean, affordable power--Canada remains an underinvested jurisdiction," the report said.

Part of the problem is weak domestic investment, which analysts say is partly thwarted by structural flaws. Top of the list, Royal Bank said, is an opaque and shifting regulatory system that extends times and increases capital costs. Royal Bank noted that, for instance, Canadian mining projects average over 20 years from discovery to production, versus over 13 years in Australia. The report added that regulatory delays and uncertainty contributed to the cancellations of eight proposed liquefied-natural-gas projects.

The Carney government has moved to reduce regulatory overlap and accelerate project approval. It made a key change this week by scaling back project assessments required for oil-and-gas pipelines and natural-gas plants.

Write to Paul Vieira at paul.vieira@wsj.com

data.title: Trump wants voters focused on Democrats, not grocery bills
data.description:
By Tim Reid

Hello, I'm Tim Reid, a Reuters national political correspondent, covering my 13th midterm election and happy to be writing my inaugural U.S. politics newsletter. This week my colleagues and I followed an unprecedented event: a national Republican Party midterms convention. Most notable about the two-day gathering in Dallas was the subject President Donald Trump and many speakers largely avoided: the cost of living and the U.S. economy, as Trump's record-low approval ratings weigh on his party's chances of keeping control of Congress.

For the past year Trump's White House aides have been urging him to hit the road and talk to voters about their number one concern: stubbornly high inflation, something the president promised he would fix when he returned to office in 2025.

In his keynote speech in Dallas on Wednesday, Trump did briefly mention inflation, repeating what he has said in speeches all year – that the term "affordability" was a Democratic "hoax", and that prices were way down since he re-entered the White House, a claim at odds with economic data.

In his nearly two-hour address, Trump barely acknowledged the strain many Americans say they feel about the cost of living. It has been a constant theme of his public addresses this year and the central problem for Republicans as they struggle to keep control of Congress in November.

Trump has cast himself as the party's chief economic messenger but his words do not match the daily reality of high grocery and gas prices for American families. As some Republicans told my colleagues Nandita Bose and Nathan Layne in Dallas, they worry about his appeal to voters to make the election a referendum on him.

The convention speech was not an outlier. In an analysis of Trump's speeches billed as economic addresses that I conducted earlier this year, I found that Trump asserted inflation had been beaten or was greatly reduced almost 20 times and said prices were falling almost 30 times.

In Dallas, Trump did make one extraordinary financial offer to voters: a $5,000 payment to every U.S. adult if Republicans win the midterms, although paying roughly $1.3 trillion into millions of bank accounts would probably increase inflation rather than lower it.

This week, Trump also pledged to send $500 checks to nearly 1 million Americans he claimed have been overcharged for government-run medical coverage. He and other speakers in Dallas also touted Trump's efforts to lower drug prices, a clear sign Republicans want to highlight the cost of health care as a political issue in the midterms.

At the Texas convention, Trump spent most of his time riffing on topics unrelated to the economy. Like many other speakers, he also turned his fire on Democrats, accusing them of being dangerously extreme.

The focus on Democrats, rather than the economy, appeared an acknowledgment by Republicans that their best chance in November is to stay largely silent on the cost of living and instead scare voters into believing a Democratic takeover of Congress would be worse for the country.

At the convention, which ended on the eve of the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, attendees marked that solemn milestone.

The first midterm campaign I covered was in 2002. With America still reeling from those attacks, President George W. Bush campaigned around the country as a wartime president, and Republicans increased their majorities in both chambers of Congress, a rare feat. This November is shaping up to be much more challenging for Republicans.

TOP US POLITICS HEADLINES

  • A year after Charlie Kirk's death, Turning Point USA grows but Trump slips with young voters

  • Analysis: Trump's Iran campaign echoes the post-9/11 'forever wars'

  • Republicans are making Muslims a campaign issue in the 2026 US midterms

  • Ash-covered shoes and a president in crisis: A Reuters reporter remembers 9/11

  • New Mexicans deride Trump's 'New America' idea

POLL OF THE WEEK

THE VIEW FROM MEXICO

Mexico and the U.S. are racing to reach a bilateral trade deal before the midterm elections, according to six sources in both countries familiar with the talks, an effort made more urgent by the collapse of Canadian trade negotiations with Washington.

The negotiations are aimed at striking an interim bilateral bargain under which Mexico could win relief from some U.S. tariffs while addressing U.S. demands on areas including automotive content and Chinese investment.

WHAT TO WATCH FOR

September 12-13: Trump travels to Ireland to watch the Irish Open golf tournament at his golf course in Doonbeg

September 22: Trump expected to address the U.N. General Assembly in New York

September 24: Trump to host Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House

data.title: US energy firms add rigs for first time in four weeks, says Baker Hughes
data.description:
By Scott DiSavino

U.S. energy firms this week added rigs for the first time in four weeks, energy services firm Baker Hughes said in its closely followed report on Friday.

The total oil and gas rig count, an early indicator of future output, rose by three to 591 in the week to September 11, its highest since mid-August. (BHGUSWTT), (BHGUSOILDRLW), (BHGUSGASDRLW)

Baker Hughes said this week's increase puts the total rig count up 52 rigs, or 10% above this time last year.

Baker Hughes said oil rigs rose by one to 450 this week, their highest since late August, while gas rigs rose by two to 132, their highest since late August, and other miscellaneous rigs held at 9.

The oil and gas rig count declined by 7% in 2025, 5% in 2024, and 20% in 2023 as lower U.S. oil prices prompted energy firms to focus more on boosting shareholder returns and paying down debt rather than increasing output.

But now with spot U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude prices expected to rise in 2026 for the first time in four years due to supply disruptions from the Iran war, the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) projected that crude output will increase from a record 13.7 million barrels per day (bpd) in 2025 to 13.8 million bpd in 2026.

On the gas side, EIA projected output will jump from a record 107.6 billion cubic feet per day (bcfd) in 2025 to 111.7 bcfd in 2026 as demand for the fuel rises to produce electricity for power-hungry data centers and liquefied natural gas (LNG) for export.

data.title: Inflation Figure Boosts Odds of Rate Hike Next Week — WSJ
data.description:
By Angus Berwick

The consumer price index rose 3.4% in August from a year ago, increasing the chances of a Federal Reserve rate hike next week to nearly 90% in traders' eyes.

The inflation figure came in the same as the prior month and as economists surveyed by the Wall Street Journal expected. But the core CPI, an inflation figure that excludes volatile food and energy prices, by some measurements was a tad stronger than expected.

The figures confirmed a narrative among investors that inflation has remained too high for the Fed to keep rates at their current level. Traders recently were putting an 89% chance on a rate increase next week.

Stocks rose, a signal that investors like the idea of a rate hike tamping down inflation. Treasury yields were mixed, with short-term yields higher and the 30-year bond yield lower.

Keeping upward pressure on prices: The cost of diesel today hit $6 a gallon for the first time. Brent crude futures were volatile, surging overnight to nearly $110 a barrel before falling back to about $105.

This item is part of a Wall Street Journal live coverage event. The full stream can be found by searching P/WSJL (WSJ Live Coverage).

data.title: Hao Feng Group, Hong Kong-Based Provider of Investment and Financial Education Programs, Files for NYSE American IPO
data.description:
Hao Feng Group filed an F-1 for its initial public offering on September 11, 2026. The Hong Kong-based investment education company plans to list on the NYSE American under the ticker “HFE,” offering 3,200,000 ordinary shares at an expected price range of $5.00 to $8.00 per share. Proceeds are earmarked for regional expansion, technology upgrades, course development, and working capital.

Business Description

Hao Feng Group is a Hong Kong-based provider of investment and financial education focused on retail and high‑net‑worth investors. Through its operating subsidiary, Hao Feng International Limited, the company delivers on‑site classes, live online sessions, and subscription‑based digital content covering topics such as trading, market analysis, portfolio construction, fundamental analysis, and options strategies. The founder and CEO is a veteran asset manager (Type 9 SFC license holder), and the curriculum blends real‑world market insights with structured learning.

The company generates revenue across three segments: on‑site educational services, subscription‑based digital content (YouTube memberships), and advertising services via sponsored video placements on its YouTube channel. Competitive strengths include a multi‑channel delivery model, an experienced tutor team, and a focus on regulatory-aligned content. Hao Feng plans to expand regionally into markets such as Malaysia, Singapore, and potentially Taiwan, while upgrading its IT stack (including CRM), broadening its course catalog, and developing proprietary algorithms and financial models to enhance instruction and personalization.

Market Overview

  • Total addressable market: Hong Kong financial education market was ~$1.05 billion in 2024, projected to reach ~$2.23 billion by 2034.
  • Market growth: 7.8% projected CAGR for Hong Kong financial education (2025–2034); 2022–2024 CAGR of 3.9%.
  • Market position: Ranked third among providers focused on retail and high-net-worth investors in Hong Kong in 2024 with ~0.15% share (BARENTSZ & CRI).
  • Key competitors: Legendary Education Group, Money Tab, FQ Education Academy, The Investopedia Institute of Hong Kong (plus regional players in Malaysia and Taiwan).
  • Industry trends: Rising retail participation, increased U.S. equities interest among Hong Kong investors, AI-driven education tools adoption, and expanding online delivery and subscription models.

Operational Metrics

  • Customers: Student headcount rose to 493 in March 2026 from 416 in March 2025; FY2025 students ~490 vs. ~430 in FY2024; over 32% of FY2025 students subscribed for more than three years.
  • Locations: One tuition center in Hong Kong (Kwun Tong).
  • Geographic presence: Primarily Hong Kong; planned expansion to Malaysia, Singapore, and potentially Taiwan.
  • Partnerships: Sponsored content with two licensed Hong Kong financial institutions (exclusive title sponsorships in Feb–Apr 2026); membership content via YouTube.
  • Other key metrics: H1 FY2026 revenue mix—On‑site education 82.3%, subscription content 3.9%, advertising 13.8%.

Financials Highlights

  • Revenue (current): $1,449,745 (FY2025); $930,216 (six months ended March 31, 2026)
  • Revenue growth: 50.1% YoY in FY2025
  • Gross profit: $1,253,513 (86.5% margin)
  • Operating income: $997,757 (FY2025 income from operations)
  • Net income: $841,144 (FY2025); $203,374 (six months ended March 31, 2026)

Management

  • Chu Chun Man, Founder, Chairman & Chief Executive Officer - Veteran asset manager with 16+ years’ experience; SFC Type 9 license holder; former fund manager at Oriens Asset Management; media contributor and investment educator.
  • Yiu Sze Man (Abby), Chief Financial Officer - Certified Public Accountant in Hong Kong; 10+ years’ finance/audit experience at PKF, Moore Stephens, JLL, and Hong Kong Arts Centre.
  • Ho Kam Chung (Wade), Independent Director - Corporate finance and legal background; former director at Anglo Chinese Corporate Finance; CFA and FRM charterholder; Principal Lawyer at Trio Partners (Australia).
  • Eliot Ames, Independent Director - Education professional with bilingual communication experience; CELTA-certified; background in program planning and student engagement.
  • Tse Lam Wai Yee (Jennie), Independent Director - Senior educator and academic affairs lead; experience in IT-enhanced teaching and assessment; TSA English Oral Examiner.

IPO Structure

  • Issuer: Hao Feng Group Ltd.
  • Filing date: September 11, 2026
  • Proposed ticker: HFE
  • Exchange: NYSE American
  • Price range: $5.00–$8.00
  • Offering size: Approximately $20.8 million at the $6.50 midpoint (3,200,000 shares; 45-day over-allotment up to 480,000 shares)
  • Shares offered: 3,200,000 Ordinary Shares (plus 480,000 over-allotment option)
  • Lead underwriters: Eddid Securities USA Inc. (Representative)
  • Use of proceeds: Global expansion (notably Malaysia, Singapore, and potentially Taiwan), IT upgrades including CRM, new course development, strengthening brand and tutor qualifications, development of self-built algorithms and financial models, and working capital.

Original SEC Filing: Hao Feng Group Ltd. - F-1 - Sep. 11, 2026

data.title: Social Security COLA Is on Pace to Rise About 3.4% for 2027 — WSJ
data.description:
By Ashlea Ebeling

With one month to go until the official estimate, Social Security recipients are on track to pocket a bigger raise in 2027 because of inflation.

If inflation climbs in line with its recent trend in the next month, recipients' monthly checks will rise by about 3.4% in 2027, according to estimates from the nonprofit Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. AARP expects a 3.6% increase. The Senior Citizens League is projecting a 3.5% increase. The estimates follow a 2.8% cost-of-living increase this year.

The annual cost-of-living increase is tied to the average inflation for July, August and September, using the Labor Department's consumer-price index for urban wage earners. The August data, released today, gives an early indication of what recipients might get when the Social Security Administration announces the official cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for 2027 in October.

With a COLA of 3.4%, the average monthly Social Security check for retired workers would rise by about $71 in January from the July average of $2,086. If the increase turns out to be 3.6%, the average monthly check would rise by about $75.

For those on Medicare, rising premiums may consume part of the COLA gains.

data.title: US court blocks Trump administration bid to keep Michigan coal plant open
data.description:
By Nichola Groom

A federal appeals court threw out a Trump administration order on Friday that had forced a Michigan coal plant to remain open beyond its planned retirement.

The unanimous ruling by a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit found the Department of Energy exceeded its authority under a rarely used emergency provision of federal law, according to court papers.

Michigan challenged the order after DOE instructed the plant in 2025 to remain online shortly before its planned closure.

The ruling is a setback for the administration's efforts to preserve coal-fired generation amid soaring U.S. demand for electricity tied to the expansion of data centers. Coal-fired power is among the largest sources of carbon dioxide emissions that contribute to climate change.

Since 2025, the Trump administration has used emergency powers under the Federal Power Act to keep several aging power plants slated for retirement operating, including coal plants in Michigan, Indiana, Washington state and Colorado.

DOE did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The decision comes a month after DOE extended the emergency order to keep the aging J.H. Campbell Generating Plant open through November 14.

The Consumers Energy plant had been slated to close in 2025 because it was no longer economic. Its continued operation under the order cost the utility $295 million from May 2025 through June 2026, according to the Michigan attorney general's office.

Consumers Energy is reviewing the ruling, spokesperson Brian Wheeler said.

"While that happens, we are continuing to comply with the current 90-day Department of Energy order that keeps the Campbell plant operating," he said.

A spokesperson for Michigan's attorney general did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“The DOE needs to stay in its lane and use its emergency powers only in actual emergencies," Michael Lenoff, an attorney with environmental group Earthjustice, said in a statement. "Preventing the market-driven retirements of coal plants to advance a coal-friendly agenda is not a proper use of emergency powers."

data.title: CDC Says Cyclospora Outbreak Is Over
data.description:
By Kelly Cloonan

Public-health officials declared an end to a cyclosporiasis outbreak that spread across the U.S. this summer.

The outbreak, which federal health officials linked to shredded iceberg lettuce from Mexican supplier Taylor Farms, has resulted in a total of 12,883 reported cases of the gastrointestinal food-borne illness across 21 states, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said Friday.

The CDC said the contaminated lettuce linked to the outbreak is no longer available in stores or restaurants, and the products' best-by dates have passed.

Additionally, recent infections linked to the outbreak have declined, with fewer than two infections per day on average in August compared to a peak of more than 1,000 daily infections, the CDC said.

The Food and Drug Administration said it continues to investigate how the product linked to the outbreak became contaminated with cyclospora, the parasite that causes cyclosporiasis.

data.title: Livestock Futures Steady Following WASDE Release — Market Talk
data.description: CME livestock futures are little changed following the release of the USDA's WASDE report. Live cattle futures remain up for the day, at 1.5% to $2.229 a pound. Meanwhile, lean hog futures remain down 1.7% to 73.075 cents a pound. The USDA projected lower production for both beef and pork in 2026, with the USDA adding in a note that its forecast includes the potential effects of new duties on Canadian goods. For beef, a slower pace of fed cattle marketings in the third quarter of 2026 is bogging down production figures, while pork output was reduced "on a slower expected pace of slaughter and lighter dressed weights." (kirk.maltais@wsj.com)

data.title: Artisan Partners Shares Fall on $6B Rebalancing From Modified Client Relationship
data.description:
By Elias Schisgall

Shares of Artisan Partners were down after the company said it expects to rebalance around $6 billion from its Global Value strategy this month as a result of a modified relationship with a client.

Shares were down 3.2% to $38.42 as of Friday afternoon. The stock has shed 5.7% so far this year.

The company said after the close Thursday that a long-standing, sub-advisory client is shifting to a multi-manager structure from a single-manager structure, with Artisan remaining as one of three managers.

The move will have a lesser impact on revenue than on assets under management, the company said, "given the nature of the mandate and its associated fee structure."

The company reported $183.5 billion in preliminary assets under management as of Aug. 31, with Artisan Funds and Artisan Global Funds making up $94.5 billion of that total.

Write to Elias Schisgall at elias.schisgall@wsj.com

data.title: Lawyer cites fake witnesses in murder case and blames ChatGPT
data.description:
Key points:
  • Lawyer's filing included invented witnesses and fabricated police testimony, court says
  • Attorney said he used ChatGPT and called the lapse an honest mistake
  • New Mexico justice said at hearing that AI hallucination risks are widely known among lawyers

By Mike Scarcella

A defense lawyer appealing his client's murder conviction submitted a brief containing made-up police testimony and witnesses fabricated by OpenAI's ChatGPT, New Mexico's highest court said.

The New Mexico Supreme Court on Wednesday fined the attorney, Stephen Aarons, and held him in contempt for failing to verify the accuracy of the court filing, which Aarons said he prepared with help from the AI program.

The filing “contained false testimony from wholly fabricated witnesses,” the court said.

The panel also said Aarons had “demonstrated a lack of remorse and a lack of concern for his client.” The justices fined Aarons $5,000 and said they will refer him to an attorney disciplinary board for investigation.

Aarons in a statement to Reuters said he had used ChatGPT to summarize the trial proceedings when he agreed to take up the defendant's appeal last year, and did not understand the degree to which AI could "hallucinate" facts.

"I am remorseful but hopeful that the disciplinary board takes into account it was an honest mistake," he said. "It is a lesson learned for all professionals who rely upon this powerful but sometimes unstable technology."

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The court’s sanction is the latest in a growing number of cases in which state and federal judges have disciplined lawyers for submitting court documents generated by AI tools without adequately vetting them. Some judges have also faced scrutiny over the use of AI.

Dozens of lawyers have been sanctioned for filing briefs where AI made up case ​citations or misquoted the law. Aarons’ filing appears to have gone further, containing fabricated witness testimony in a criminal appeal.

Aarons, a private attorney based in Santa Fe, was handling the appeal of Oscar Renee Sandoval, who pleaded not guilty to the murder of the mother of his children before he was convicted and sentenced last year to life in prison.

The appeal is still pending and was assigned on September 2 to Kim Chavez Cook, a New Mexico public defender. Cook declined to comment.

The district attorney's office for Doña Ana County also declined to comment.

The state supreme court last month ordered Aarons to explain how the fabricated material, which it said appeared to include "fictional statements that the shooter was wearing dark pants and a white shirt," was included in his primary brief in the appeal.

Aarons told the court at an August 21 hearing that he fed a computer-generated transcript and other case materials to ChatGPT, presuming it would generate "a bulletproof summary."

The justices sounded incredulous that Aarons was not fully aware of how AI can make mistakes.

"Counsel, do you watch the news? Do you listen to the radio? Do you read anything about what's going on in the world?" Justice C. Shannon Bacon said at the hearing. "Because the problem with lawyers relying on AI hallucinations is an above-the-fold story every single day.”
